solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Spear a fish

blocks.note: first meaning: a long infantry weapon with a pointed head on a pole
second meaning: a large predatory freshwater fish

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as an instruction to go spearfishing, but there is no verb at all: two nouns sit side by side, each a meaning of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a medieval pole weapon carried by foot soldiers and a long-jawed predatory fish of rivers and lakes.

clue.text: Icy home has one grand toilet

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
G is the usual abbreviation for grand, a thousand pounds
loo is the everyday British word for a toilet

explanation.surface: A frozen dwelling boasts one rather splendid lavatory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grand' looks like an adjective praising the toilet, but it is a thousand pounds, abbreviated to one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An Inuit dome-shaped shelter is built from blocks of packed snow, so it is literally a dwelling made of ice.

clue.text: Key slang for “snail”

blocks.note: the Escape key on a computer keyboard, labelled Esc
argot is the jargon or slang of a particular group

explanation.surface: Someone asks what the slang term for a snail is.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'snail' look like the word being translated, but it is simply the definition; the key is a computer one, not a musical key.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the French word for an edible snail, used on menus for the cooked dish in garlic butter.

clue.text: I must leave Toledo area for Englishman’s home, they say

indicators.note: something that must leave has to go away, so a letter is dropped from the word

blocks.note: taken as written
Toledo lies in Castile, the historic central region of Spain

explanation.surface: Someone has to quit the Spanish city of Toledo and head back to England.
explanation.walkthrough: Castile (in full, Castilla-La Mancha) is the Spanish region around Toledo; taking out its I leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says an Englishman's home is his castle, meaning a private domain; 'they say' flags that the definition is a well-known saying.

clue.text: Feel sorry for rook and heron

blocks.note: R is the chess notation for a rook
an egret is a kind of white heron

explanation.surface: Someone pities two birds, a rook and a heron.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rook' reads as a crow alongside the heron, but here it is the chess piece, abbreviated to one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To feel sorry about something you did is to wish it undone, which is what this verb describes.

clue.text: Story young girl lisped

indicators.note: a lisp turns an S sound into TH, so we hear the word as a lisping speaker would pronounce it

blocks.note: a young girl is a miss; said with a lisp, miss comes out as mith

explanation.surface: A little girl tells a story with a lisp.
explanation.walkthrough: Miss is the young girl; lisped, its final S becomes TH, matching the sound of a legendary tale.
explanation.definitionFit: A traditional tale about gods or heroes is a kind of story, and the word also covers any widely held fiction.

clue.text: In emergency driver may use this, for a change

definitions.text: In emergency driver may use this, for a change

blocks.clueFragment: In emergency driver may use this
blocks.note: surface reading: something a motorist reaches for when stuck at the roadside
setter's reading: the item is literally kept to be changed onto the car after a puncture

explanation.walkthrough: 'For a change' sounds like 'for once, unusually', but it is literal: the item exists for changing a wheel. Tyre is the British spelling of tire.
explanation.definitionFit: Cars carry an extra wheel in the boot precisely so a driver can fit it after a puncture.

clue.text: Cut out PE without a sign of hesitation

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the second piece is taken away from the first

blocks.note: PE stands for physical education, school exercise
er is the sound people make when hesitating

explanation.surface: A school decides to drop PE without a moment's hesitation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut out PE' looks like one instruction about scrapping gym class; in fact 'Cut out' is the definition and PE is expanded to the word it abbreviates.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgeons remove tissue by cutting it away, and this verb is the formal medical term for that removal.

clue.text: Big league of countries, initially — with common interests

definitions.text: Big league of countries, initially — with common interests

indicators.note: initially points to the start, so only the opening letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: the leading letters of the four words

explanation.surface: A large alliance of nations shares common interests.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: its first four words supply the letters and, read entire, describe the thing itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of nations allied by shared political or economic aims, such as the former Soviet one, is called this.

clue.text: Tremor, following second white wine

blocks.note: following means coming after
S is the abbreviation for second
hock is the British name for German white wine from the Rhine

explanation.surface: Someone gets the shakes after a second glass of white wine.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a hangover tremble, but the tremor is seismic. Hock is the old British name for Rhine wine.
explanation.definitionFit: A smaller earthquake felt after the main one is a tremor of the ground, so the word fits as a specific kind.

clue.text: Rise rapidly and so far heartlessly

indicators.note: without a heart means with the centre taken out, so the middle letter goes

blocks.note: taken as written, run together

explanation.surface: Prices have climbed quickly and, up to now, without mercy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'So far' reads as 'up to now', but the two words are joined and their central F removed.
explanation.definitionFit: To fly or climb steeply upward, like a bird or a share price, is what this verb describes.

clue.text: Supposed, we hear, hotel by Yorkshire river is a small one

definitions.note: 'one' stands for hotel, mentioned earlier in the clue

indicators.note: what we hear is spoken, so the word is taken by its sound rather than its spelling
by means beside, so the pieces sit next to each other

blocks.note: supposed means guessed, which sounds like a hotel visitor
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
the Ouse flows through York

explanation.surface: A hotel beside a Yorkshire river is reportedly a small one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hotel' seems to be what is being described, but it only supplies a letter; the definition at the end uses 'one' to point back to it.
explanation.definitionFit: A modest private lodging house taking paying visitors is essentially a small hotel, often family-run.

clue.text: Weaken, to cut a long story short

indicators.note: to cut something is to remove part of it, so a letter is dropped
cut short means docked at the end, so the final letter is lost

blocks.note: a saga is a long story

explanation.surface: A familiar phrase for getting to the point of a tale.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'to cut a long story short' is taken literally: a long story is trimmed of its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To droop or lose strength, as a rope or flagging energy does, is a sense of weakening.

clue.text: Officially noted as available to play

blocks.note: first meaning: formally documented, publicly stated
second meaning: pressed onto a disc, so music can be played back

explanation.walkthrough: 'Available to play' sounds like a fit sports player; read literally it is music held on a gramophone disc.
explanation.definitionFit: A formally logged statement is documented, and a song pressed onto vinyl can be played back, both covered by this phrase.

clue.text: Try a story, number one

blocks.note: to have a go is to try
taken as written
a story can be a fib, a lie

explanation.surface: Someone attempts a tale for the top spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Story' means a fib here, not a tale.
explanation.definitionFit: In football the keeper traditionally wears shirt 1, so the team's first-choice keeper is its number one.

clue.text: Liquor salesman who avoids all duties?

blocks.note: first meaning: a seller of illicit alcohol
second meaning: a smuggler who pays no customs or excise taxes on goods

explanation.walkthrough: 'Duties' suggests chores or responsibilities; here it means customs and excise taxes, which a smuggler evades. The question mark marks the playful second definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who makes or sells illegal alcohol, famously during US Prohibition, dodges the taxes levied on it.

clue.text: Very bad feelings in university in eastern New York

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: MIT is the Massachusetts Institute of Technology
E is the abbreviation for eastern
NY is the standard abbreviation for New York

explanation.surface: There is real hostility at a college on the US east coast.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'in' links definition to wordplay; the second puts the university inside the state's abbreviation, after the E.
explanation.definitionFit: Deep mutual hostility between people or nations is ill will, a very bad feeling held over time.

clue.text: Look with astonishment, at this box?

definitions.note: the word is the first half of a compound naming the box

blocks.note: first meaning: stare wide-eyed in amazement
second meaning: British slang calls the television the box people stare at, naming it after the staring verb

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a looser second definition: goggle-box is British slang for the television, the box people sit staring at.
explanation.definitionFit: To stare with wide, bulging eyes, as in amazement, is the meaning of this verb, and it prefixes the slang name for a TV set.

clue.text: Fruit, but no starter, for all

indicators.note: with no starter there is no opening, so the first letter is removed

blocks.note: a peach is a stone fruit

explanation.surface: A meal offers fruit for everyone but no first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' looks like a menu course, but it means the first letter of the fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: As in 'two pounds apiece', the word distributes a price or share to every one, so it means per item, for all.

clue.text: Resounding noise as family essentially argue

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its core, so only its centre letter is used

blocks.note: a clan is an extended family
the central letter of the five

explanation.surface: A loud din breaks out when the family quarrels.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a domestic row; the noise is metallic, and 'argue' gives only its central letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The loud ringing sound of metal struck against metal is a resounding noise, like a dropped pan.

clue.text: British have no charm: this is diabolical

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for British
to lack is to have none
a charm is a magic spell, and magic is charm

explanation.surface: Someone complains that the British are utterly lacking in charm, which is appalling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diabolical' suggests a grumble about manners, but 'this is diabolical' points to something of the devil itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Sorcery that calls on evil spirits is satanic, of the devil, which is what diabolical literally means.

clue.text: Huge nation lacking a feature

indicators.note: lacking means going without, so a letter is left out

blocks.note: China is one of the largest countries
taken as written

explanation.surface: A vast country lacks some notable characteristic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feature' reads as a characteristic of a nation; it is a part of the face.
explanation.definitionFit: Facial features are the parts of the face such as nose, eyes and the jut below the mouth.

clue.text: Old fellow’s country

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
a fellow is a man

explanation.walkthrough: The possessive suggests the country belongs to the old fellow; in the parse it simply joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This sultanate on the south-east tip of the Arabian Peninsula is a sovereign nation.

clue.text: Reader of lesson always carries gun

indicators.note: to carry something is to hold it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, meaning always
a pistol is a handgun

explanation.surface: A church reader who never goes without a firearm.
explanation.walkthrough: The lesson is a Bible reading in church, specifically from one of the New Testament letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In church services, the person who reads the Epistle, a New Testament letter, aloud is given this title.

clue.text: Appreciates lodgings

blocks.note: first meaning: likes or enjoys, in informal speech
second meaning: rented rooms, especially a student's

explanation.walkthrough: The verb and the noun look unrelated; one is slang for liking something, the other British slang for rented rooms.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang 'dig' means enjoy, as in 'he really digs jazz', and British slang uses the plural noun for rented rooms.
